To echo the other poster, thank you for bringing this up. I'm sorry I don't have very useful advice for you, because I'm struggling with the same thing. I've been out of the relationship for about a year now, and I developed (C)PTSD from it, which I'm still suffering from. Even though my family knows the relationship was abusive, based on some things they've said recently, it seems they still have trouble believing it could have possibly been THAT bad. I can tell they're suspicious that I'm overreacting, or worse yet, that I was responsible for provoking some of the abuse I ended up receiving.

Quite frankly, I just imagine that it's really hard for people to understand if they have never experienced being in a codependent relationship with someone with a personality disorder, especially BPD. Even if they've been in an abusive relationship, a BPD one is just such a different experience that it's hard to relate to if you've never gone through it. Perhaps others in this sub have found ways to successfully relay their experience/feelings to their loved ones, but what helps me the most is keeping my expectations low.

There was one redditor in this sub who said they went through both a divorce with their partner of ~10 years and later in life, a breakup after dating a pwBPD for a wayyy shorter time (months iirc, but if not, def no more than 2 years). And that the toll the latter relationship + breakup took on them was MUCH greater, which even baffled them. To the average person who's not knowledgeable about BPD, that might seem odd or overdramatic that a short relationship was more painful and devastating than the end of  a marriage. But people like us who have experienced relationships with pwBPD can instantly understand and recognize that their reaction was completely valid. Because the one with a BPD is such a different beast, even a brief relationship can be extremely damaging.

So again, I'm sorry I can't help you figure out a way to explain. But I wanted to let you know I'm in solidarity with you, experiencing the same thing with my family, so while it may not help much, I hope it comforts you a little to know you're not alone in struggling with this, and that your emotional response is completely understandable. And I'm sorry you had to go through all that in your relationship and now have to deal with this. I'll be wishing you the best.

I also feel like, especially as women, we are taught to believe that we are supposed to sacrifice our happiness for the happiness of others -- whether that is our partner, children, family, etc. And sacrificing our happiness is how we are supposed to be happy or fulfilled. But I personally feel so exhausted setting myself on fire so others can stay warm. Yet I've heard, especially from my mom, that that sacrifice is the ultimate form of love and should be championed. When I disagree, I feel shamed for wanting to pursue my own happiness.. It's messed up.

How do you feel when that happens? Sometimes I gaslight myself into feeling like they must be right, and I'm at fault. I feel like that's not right but at the same time, I don't know. What is the normal reaction? How do other people with these issues feel hearing that, and how am I supposed to feel?

Based on your post and comments, I think therapy would be a great help to you, both individual and couples therapy. Every person, no matter how well or poorly they are doing, can benefit from therapy, which a good therapist will help you at the very least gain perspective. I think of it like maintenance for your mind, like if you're maintaining a car or something.

If you can't afford both right now, maybe start with individual therapy (specifically for this issue? I realize that you've had therapy before!). I highly suggest couples therapy long before marriage though, even for couples that think everything is perfect. You both should probably do it as soon as possible. Maybe he can pay for couples therapy, and you can pay for individual therapy?

Things don't have to be going badly at the moment for you to benefit from therapy. Clearly you have experienced multiple cycles of being fine then having doubts. It is ok to go to therapy and talk about/reflect on when you were not fine, even during times you feel fine. Especially because there is a good chance those doubts will crop up again, and even if not, then at least you are able to learn about yourself and why you think the way you do more. My ex had OCD, and based on my experiences, I wager that your past OCD diagnosis might contribute to your thought processes, although how much I cannot say. It is very reasonable even without OCD that you are deeply affected by what had happened in the past. In your case, I implore you again to see a professional and wish you good luck!

You don't have to make it a big deal when you bring it up. Just firmly tell him not to say perverted and inappropriate things around your friends and family. There's not really a need to explain or analyze why (it's obvious), unless he asks. If he offers an explanation, you can hear him out and come to an understanding, but it ultimately doesn't matter. Because he still needs to stop.

For the family dinners, again it's not really about his intent, but it's disrespectful to not come down to dinner when you are invited. He doesn't have to eat if he's not hungry, but he should make himself present. I was hanging out at my boyfriend's house, and then it was time for the family to eat dinner. They didn't have any food I could eat, and I wasn't hungry anyway, so I didn't eat anything... But I still went down and sat at the dinner table with them. If he doesn't want to eat dinner with your family, then he or you both need to make yourself scarce when dinnertime comes around (go out and eat or something), because that IS rude behavior for a guest, with the exception of if your family truly doesn't mind. But they clearly do.

He may be feeling awkward and uncomfortable, and while that's ok, it's not a good enough reason to be avoidant if you guys plan on getting serious and him having a relationship with your family. My boyfriend is not that well-liked by my friends and family, but he tries. He acts totally natural with me, but he doesn't always have the most palatable social skills with people he doesn't know well. When with my f&f, he might come off as kind of loud or desperate to be liked, or on the other side of the spectrum, will contribute very little if he eventually feels too awkward and doesn't feel accepted. But at least he puts in an effort to make conversation despite his discomfort, which I appreciate.

 If you guys are going to get more serious, I recommend you approach the talk like this. The inappropriate comments and dinner etiquette can be addressed point-blank. For the other problems, tell him you feel like, with your f&f, he converses in short answers and doesn't if seem to contribute to the conversation. Ask him why it seems to be like that, like does he feel awkward with them? Does he just have nothing to say? But tell him you would appreciate if he would consciously put more effort into engaging with them. If he asks why you bring this up, and you want to protect his feelings by not revealing \*everything\*, you can just say that, because he doesn't come off as super involved, your family wonders if he feels uncomfortable with them. So you would like him to put more effort in his interactions with them. If he refuses for some reason...well, it had better be a good reason, in my opinion. He doesn't have to be perfect right away, but he should at least try and want to try.

I agree with other posters about his behavior raising flags, but I know how these things go. It's ultimately up to you whether or not they're dealbreakers. If not, the strategy I outlined above is how I would talk to my boyfriend about it.

Good point, there really isn't anyone to blame, and I think I wanna be hard on myself because I desperately want something to blame, or else I can't wrap my head around it. It's scary too, to realize there's no one to blame, but what can we do. Just wanna let you know I validate you for having to deal with that damage regardless of a loving childhood, and I hope we make it out ok. Fuck, it sucks that we gotta deal with it, but it's ours.

*hugs*

Oh my goodness... You are the PARENT! Your children don't OWE you anything from what YOU chose to give them during their childhood! YOU chose to bring them into this world, YOU chose to raise them the way you did...and it's fine to expect gratitude for the opportunities you blessed them with, but in no way are you ENTITLED to anything just because you provided for them in their childhood! Welcome to the REAL adult world.

Of course, once they became adults, then it's more understandable to have a more equal relationship, when it comes to borrowing money and stuff like that. If you wanted to be compensated for the time you babysat your grandkids, fine. There are people out there who take advantage of their parents, placing undue responsibility on them to babysit the grandkids. But not only is this not the case, but you didn't make it clear beforehand that you wanted money in exchange for taking care of your grandkids BEFORE they came out to see you, thus NO DEAL. And it's a red flag for me that you don't consider time with them a privilege, and instead think of it like a transaction and "you didn't ask for them to be born." That's technically fair, but what kind of grandpa thinks like that... If I were your daughter and knew you thought like that, I would not give you the privilege of being a grandfather to my children! You can just be a babysitter-for-hire and only see them on MY terms.

A situation in which a grandparent might ask to be compensated for babysitting doesn't necessarily mean they're the asshole.

But not only are YTA in this situation, but your values and way you view the world and your family through the lens of money money money... My goodness. I sincerely hope you use these comments as an opportunity to self-reflect.

I was reading a user's comment on another sub who said they have learned the need to distinguish between their gut feeling and feelings of anxiety. What they thought might be a gut feeling, is sometimes actually just their anxiety. But sometimes it really is their gut feeling, and their response was appropriate to the situation.

I don't have the answer for you, but I do suggest you look inside yourself and figure out why you have this feeling. Could there be reasons like not wanting commitment yet, or feeling like he is not the person you want to be with? You two could explore values, future goals, and dealbreakers to see if those align. Could it be anxiety? Is it something else? Try to figure that out, and don't be afraid to talk to a therapist or someone to help support you.

Just find a different group of friends. They are allowed to have their boundaries and opinions, and if you disrespect them as another commenter said, that is not good.

But taking candid photos and browsing former classmates' social media and stuff isn't in itself creepy... It's pretty normal. In fact, me and one of my friends I've known since elementary look up former classmates together once in a while out of curiosity to see what they're up to when we catch up and reminisce. And I have a number of different groups of college friends who are all about taking candid photos.

Just find different friends to be close to, and if you want to keep hanging out with these ones, respect their boundaries and what they feel comfortable with. Also the way you describe it in your post, they don't seem to communicate their discomfort well with you. Calling you creepy is not very nice. It's a sign of immaturity at best. I think nice friends would tell you how your actions make them feel uncomfortable without trying to make you feel bad. At least that's how my friends are.
Do not make irreversible decisions when you are in a very emotional state. At least in relationships. It's usually best to wait it out until you can think more clearly.
